verses.zh: 看哪，耶和华使地空虚，变为荒凉；又翻转大地，将居民分散。
verses.en: Look, the Lord is ready to devastate the earthand leave it in ruins;he will mar its surfaceand scatter its inhabitants.

verses.zh: 那时百姓怎样，祭司也怎样；仆人怎样，主人也怎样；婢女怎样，主母也怎样；买物的怎样，卖物的也怎样；放债的怎样，借债的也怎样；取利的怎样，出利的也怎样。
verses.en: Everyone will suffer—the priest as well as the people,[NOTE:1] the master as well as the servant,[NOTE:2] the elegant lady as well as the female attendant,[NOTE:3] the seller as well as the buyer,[NOTE:4] the borrower as well as the lender,[NOTE:5] the creditor as well as the debtor.[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “and it will be like the people, like the priest.”
Heb “like the servant, like his master.”
Heb “like the female servant, like her mistress.”
Heb “like the buyer, like the seller.”
Heb “like the lender, like the borrower.”
Heb “like the creditor, just as the one to whom he lends.”

verses.zh: 地必全然空虚，尽都荒凉；因为这话是耶和华说的。
verses.en: The earth will be completely devastatedand thoroughly ransacked.For the Lord has decreed this judgment.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “for the Lord has spoken this word.”

verses.zh: 地上悲哀衰残，世界败落衰残；地上居高位的人也败落了。
verses.en: The earth[NOTE:1] dries up[NOTE:2] and withers,the world shrivels up and withers;the prominent people of the earth[NOTE:3] fade away.
notes: Some prefer to read “land” here, but the word pair אֶרֶץ/תֵּבֵל (ʾerets/tevel [see the corresponding term in the parallel line]) elsewhere clearly designates the earth/world (see 1 Sam 2:8; 1 Chr 16:30; Job 37; 12; Pss 19:4; 24:1; 33:8; 89:11; 90:2; 96:13; 98:9; Prov 8:26, 31; Isa 14:16-17; 34:1; Jer 10:12; 51:15; Lam 4:12). According to L. Stadelmann, תבל designates “the habitable part of the world” (The Hebrew Conception of the World [AnBib], 130).
Or “mourns” (BDB 5 s.v. אָבַל). HALOT 6-7 lists the homonyms I אבל (“mourn”) and II אבל (“dry up”). They propose the second here on the basis of parallelism.

Heb “the height of the people of the earth.” The translation assumes an emendation of the singular form מְרוֹם (merom, “height of”) to the plural construct מְרֹמֵי (merome, “high ones of”; note the plural verb at the beginning of the line), and understands the latter as referring to the prominent people of human society.

verses.zh: 地被其上的居民污秽；因为他们犯了律法，废了律例，背了永约。
verses.en: The earth is defiled by[NOTE:1] its inhabitants,[NOTE:2] for they have violated laws,disregarded the regulation,[NOTE:3] and broken the permanent treaty.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “beneath”; cf. KJV, ASV, NRSV “under”; NAB “because of.”
Isa 26:21 suggests that the earth’s inhabitants defiled the earth by shedding the blood of their fellow human beings. See also Num 35:33-34, which assumes that bloodshed defiles a land.
Heb “moved past [the?] regulation.”

Or “everlasting covenant” (KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT); NAB “the ancient covenant”; CEV “their agreement that was to last forever.”sn For a lengthy discussion of the identity of this covenant/treaty, see R. Chisholm, “The ‘Everlasting Covenant’ and the ‘City of Chaos’: Intentional Ambiguity and Irony in Isaiah 24, ” CTR 6 (1993): 237-53. In this context, where judgment comes upon both the pagan nations and God’s covenant community, the phrase “permanent treaty” is intentionally ambiguous. For the nations this treaty is the Noahic mandate of Gen 9:1-7 with its specific stipulations and central regulation (Gen 9:7). By shedding blood, the warlike nations violated this treaty, which promotes population growth and prohibits murder. For Israel, which was also guilty of bloodshed (see Isa 1:15, 21; 4:4), this “permanent treaty” would refer more specifically to the Mosaic Law and its regulations prohibiting murder (Exod 20:13; Num 35:6-34), which are an extension of the Noahic mandate.

verses.zh: 所以，地被咒诅吞灭；住在其上的显为有罪。地上的居民被火焚烧，剩下的人稀少。
verses.en: So a treaty curse[NOTE:1] devours the earth;its inhabitants pay for their guilt.[NOTE:2] This is why the inhabitants of the earth disappear,[NOTE:3] and are reduced to just a handful of people.[NOTE:4]
notes: Ancient Near Eastern treaties often had “curses,” or threatened judgments, attached to them. (See Deut 28 for a biblical example of such curses.) The party or parties taking an oath of allegiance acknowledged that disobedience would activate these curses, which typically threatened loss of agricultural fertility as depicted in the following verses.
The verb אָשַׁם (ʾasham, “be guilty”) is here used metonymically to mean “pay, suffer for one’s guilt” (see HALOT 95 s.v. אשׁם).

BDB 359 s.v. חָרַר derives the verb חָרוּ (kharu) from חָרַר (kharar, “burn”), but HALOT 351 s.v. II חרה understands a hapax legomenon חָרָה (kharah, “to diminish in number,” a homonym of חָרָה) here, relating it to an alleged Arabic cognate meaning “to decrease.” The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has חורו, perhaps understanding the root as חָוַר (khavar, “grow pale”; see Isa 29:22 and HALOT 299 s.v. I חור).
Heb “and mankind is left small [in number].”

verses.zh: 新酒悲哀，葡萄树衰残；心中欢乐的俱都叹息。
verses.en: The new wine dries up,the vines shrivel up,all those who like to celebrate[NOTE:1] groan.
notes: The Hebrew text reads literally, “all the joyful in heart,” but the context specifies the context as parties and drinking bouts.

verses.zh: 击鼓之乐止息；宴乐人的声音完毕，弹琴之乐也止息了。
verses.en: The happy sound[NOTE:1] of the tambourines stops,the revelry of those who celebrate comes to a halt,the happy sound of the harp ceases.
notes: Heb “the joy” (again later in this verse).

verses.zh: 人必不得饮酒唱歌；喝浓酒的，必以为苦。
verses.en: They no longer sing and drink wine;[NOTE:1] the beer tastes bitter to those who drink it.
notes: Heb “with a song they do not drink wine.”

verses.zh: 荒凉的城拆毁了；各家关门闭户，使人都不得进去。
verses.en: The ruined town[NOTE:1] is shattered;all the houses are shut up tight.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “the city of chaos” (so NAB, NASB, NRSV). Isaiah uses the term תֹּהוּ (tohu) rather frequently of things (like idols) that are empty and worthless (see BDB 1062 s.v.), so the word might characterize the city as rebellious or morally worthless. However, in this context, which focuses on the effects of divine judgment, it probably refers to the ruined or worthless condition in which the city is left (note the use of the word in Isa 34:11). For a discussion of the identity of this city, see R. Chisholm, “The ‘Everlasting Covenant’ and the ‘City of Chaos’: Intentional Ambiguity and Irony in Isaiah 24, ” CTR 6 (1993): 237-53. In the context of universal judgment depicted in Isa 24, this city represents all the nations and cities of the world which, like Babylon of old and the powers/cities mentioned in chapters 13-23, rebel against God’s authority. Behind the stereotypical language one can detect various specific manifestations of this symbolic and paradigmatic city, including Babylon, Moab, and Jerusalem, all of which are alluded or referred to in chapters 24-27.
Heb “every house is closed up from entering.”

verses.zh: 在街上因酒有悲叹的声音；一切喜乐变为昏暗；地上的欢乐归于无有。
verses.en: They howl in the streets because of what happened to the wine;[NOTE:1] all joy turns to sorrow;[NOTE:2] celebrations disappear from the earth.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “[there is] an outcry over the wine in the streets.”
Heb “all joy turns to evening,” the darkness of evening symbolizing distress and sorrow.
Heb “the joy of the earth disappears.”

verses.zh: 城中只有荒凉；城门拆毁净尽。
verses.en: The city is left in ruins;[NOTE:1] the gate is reduced to rubble.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and there is left in the city desolation.”
Heb “and [into] rubble the gate is crushed.”

verses.zh: 在地上的万民中，必像打过的橄榄树，又像已摘的葡萄所剩无几。
verses.en: This is what will happen throughout[NOTE:1] the earth,among the nations.It will be like when they beat an olive tree,and just a few olives are left at the end of the harvest.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “in the midst of” (so KJV, ASV, NASB).
The judgment will severely reduce the earth’s population. See v. 6.

verses.zh: 这些人要高声欢呼；他们为耶和华的威严，从海那里扬起声来。
verses.en: They[NOTE:1] lift their voices and shout joyfully;they praise[NOTE:2] the majesty of the Lord in the west.
notes: The remnant of the nations (see v. 13) may be the unspecified subject. If so, then those who have survived the judgment begin to praise God.
Heb “they yell out concerning.”

verses.zh: 因此，你们要在东方荣耀耶和华，在众海岛荣耀耶和华―以色列　神的名。
verses.en: So in the east[NOTE:1] extol the Lord,along the seacoasts extol[NOTE:2] the fame[NOTE:3] of the Lord God of Israel.
notes: The Hebrew text reads literally, “in the lights,” interpreted by some to mean “in the region of light,” referring to the east. Some scholars have suggested the emendation of בָּאֻרִים (baʾurim) to בְּאִיֵּי הַיָּם (beʾiyye hayyam, “along the seacoasts”), a phrase that is repeated in the next line. In this case, the two lines form synonymous parallelism. If one retains the MT reading (as above), “in the east” and “along the seacoasts” depict the two ends of the earth to refer to all the earth (as a merism).
The word “extol” is supplied in the translation; the verb in the first line does double duty in the parallelism.
Heb “name,” which here stands for God’s reputation achieved by his mighty deeds.

verses.zh: 我们听见从地极有人歌唱，说：荣耀归于义人。我却说：我消灭了！我消灭了，我有祸了！诡诈的行诡诈；诡诈的大行诡诈。
verses.en: From the ends of the earth we[NOTE:1] hear songs—the Just One is majestic.[NOTE:2] But I[NOTE:3] say, “I’m wasting away! I’m wasting away! I’m doomed!Deceivers deceive, deceivers thoroughly deceive!”[NOTE:4]
notes: The identity of the subject is unclear. Apparently in vv. 15-16a an unidentified group responds to the praise they hear in the west by exhorting others to participate.
Heb “Beauty belongs to the just one.” These words may summarize the main theme of the songs mentioned in the preceding line.
The prophet seems to contradict what he hears the group saying. Their words are premature because more destruction is coming.

Heb “and [with] deception deceivers deceive.”tn Verse 16b is a classic example of Hebrew wordplay. In the first line (“I’m wasting away….”) four consecutive words end with hireq yod ( ִי); in the second line all forms are derived from the root בָּגַד (bagad). The repetition of sound draws attention to the prophet’s lament.

verses.zh: 地上的居民哪，恐惧、陷坑、网罗都临近你。
verses.en: Terror, pit, and snareare ready to overtake you, inhabitants of the earth![NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “[are] upon you, O inhabitant of the earth.” The first line of v. 17 provides another classic example of Hebrew wordplay. The names of the three instruments of judgment (פָח,פַחַת ,פַּחַד [pakhad, fakhat, fakh]) all begin with the letters פ and ח (pe and khet) and the first two end in dental consonants (ד and ת, dalet and tav). Once again the repetition of sound draws attention to the statement and contributes to the theme of the inescapability of judgment. As their similar-sounding names suggest, terror, pit, and snare are allies in destroying the objects of divine wrath.

verses.zh: 躲避恐惧声音的必坠入陷坑；从陷坑上来的必被网罗缠住；因为天上的窗户都开了，地的根基也震动了。
verses.en: The one who runs away from the sound of the terrorwill fall into the pit;[NOTE:1] the one who climbs out of the pitwill be trapped by the snare.For the floodgates of the heavens[NOTE:2] are opened up[NOTE:3] and the foundations of the earth shake.
notes: The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.
Heb “from the height”; KJV “from on high.”
The language reflects the account of the Noahic Flood (see Gen 7:11).

verses.zh: 地全然破坏，尽都崩裂，大大地震动了。
verses.en: The earth is broken in pieces,the earth is ripped to shreds,the earth shakes violently.[NOTE:1]
notes: Once more repetition is used to draw attention to a statement. In the Hebrew text each line ends with אֶרֶץ (ʾerets, “earth”). Each line also uses a Hitpolel verb form from a geminate root preceded by an emphatic infinitive absolute.

verses.zh: 地要东倒西歪，好像醉酒的人；又摇来摇去，好像吊床。罪过在其上沉重，必然塌陷，不能复起。
verses.en: The earth will stagger around[NOTE:1] like a drunk;it will sway back and forth like a hut in a windstorm.[NOTE:2] Its sin will weigh it down,and it will fall and never get up again.
notes: Heb “staggering, staggers.” The Hebrew text uses the infinitive absolute before the finite verb for emphasis and sound play.
The words “in a windstorm” are supplied in the translation to clarify the metaphor.

verses.zh: 到那日，耶和华在高处必惩罚高处的众军，在地上必惩罚地上的列王。
verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] the Lord will punish[NOTE:2] the heavenly forces in the heavens[NOTE:3] and the earthly kings on the earth.
notes: Or “in that day” (so KJV). The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.
Heb “visit [in judgment].”

Heb “the host of the height in the height.” The “host of the height/heaven” refers to the heavenly luminaries (stars and planets; see, among others, Deut 4:19; 17:3; 2 Kgs 17:16; 21:3, 5; 23:4-5; 2 Chr 33:3, 5) that populate the divine/heavenly assembly in mythological and prescientific Israelite thought (see Job 38:7; Isa 14:13).

verses.zh: 他们必被聚集，像囚犯被聚在牢狱中，并要囚在监牢里，多日之后便被讨罪（或译：眷顾）。
verses.en: They will be imprisoned in a pit,[NOTE:1] locked up in a prison,and after staying there for a long time,[NOTE:2] they will be punished.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “they will be gathered [in] a gathering [as] a prisoner in a cistern.” It is tempting to eliminate אֲסֵפָה (ʾasefah, “a gathering”) as dittographic or as a gloss, but sound repetition is one of the main characteristics of the style of this section of the chapter.
Heb “and after a multitude of days.”

Heb “visited” (so KJV, ASV). This verse can mean to visit for good or for evil. The translation assumes the latter, based on v. 21a. However, BDB 823 s.v. פָּקַד B.Niph.2 suggests the meaning “visit graciously” here, in which case one might translate “they will be released.”

verses.zh: 那时，月亮要蒙羞，日头要惭愧；因为万军之耶和华必在锡安山，在耶路撒冷作王；在敬畏他的长老面前，必有荣耀。
verses.en: The full moon will be covered up,[NOTE:1] the bright sun[NOTE:2] will be darkened;[NOTE:3] for the Lord of Heaven’s Armies will rule[NOTE:4] on Mount Zion in Jerusalem[NOTE:5] in the presence of his assembly, in majestic splendor.[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “will be ashamed.”
Or “glow of the sun.”
Heb “will be ashamed” (so NCV).
Or “take his throne,” “become king.”
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Heb “and before his elders [in] splendor.”

Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

BACKGROUND STUDY

- Isaiah 24-27 (often called "the Isaiah Apocalypse") forms a literary unit related to the end-time (i.e. world judgment). This particular genre in
Isaiah (which set the literary stage for the development of apocalyptic genre) is a pattern of end-time
blessings and judgments interwoven, much like Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-28. Isaiah 24 speaks
of God's universal judgment on the earth, while Isaiah 25 speaks of the entire earth being blessed by
a restored Zion (cf. Isa. 2:2-24). This swing of judgment and blessing is characteristic of the prophet.

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

- Isaiah 13-23 shows God's judgment on the surrounding nations that affected the people of God.
Isaiah 24-27 is an obvious conclusion to this literary unit. This same concluding genre can be seen
in Isa. 34 and 35.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ISAIAH 24:1-6

1Behold, the Lord lays the earth waste, devastates
it, distorts its surface and scatters its inhabitants. 2And the people will be like the priest, the servant like his master, the
maid like her mistress, the buyer like the seller, the lender like the borrower, the creditor like the debtor. 3The earth will
be completely laid waste and completely despoiled, for the Lord has spoken this word. 4The
earth mourns and withers, the world fades and withers, the exalted of the people of the earth fade away. 5The
earth is also polluted by its inhabitants, for they transgressed laws, violated statutes, broke the everlasting covenant. 6Therefore,
a curse devours the earth, and those who live in it are held guilty. Therefore, the inhabitants of the earth are burned, and few men are left.

24:1 "the Lord lays the earth waste" Verses 1 and 3 use a series of strong VERBS
to describe YHWH's judgment on the earth (not "land" here because of parallel to "world" [BDB 385, cf.
Isa. 14:16-17; 34:1; Jer. 10:12; 51:15], see Special Topic following).

- lays. . .waste, Isa. 24:1, BDB 132, KB 150, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE,
cf. Isa. 24:3; Nah. 2:2

- devastates, Isa. 24:1, BDB 118, KB 135, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, cf. Nah. 2:10

- distorts (lit. "twists," cf. NRSV), BDB 730, KB 796, Piel PERFECT
with waw

- scatters, Isa. 24:1, BDB 806, KB 918, Hiphil PERFECT with waw

- completely laid waste, Isa. 24:3, BDB 132, KB 150, Niphal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root denote intensity

- completely despoiled, Isa. 24:3, BDB 102, KB 117, Niphal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root denotes intensity.
YHWH takes back His gifts, given in creation (cf. Isa. 24:5-6). This is a reversal of the
purpose of original creation, but a faithful remnant will survive (cf. Isa. 24:6)!

Verses 1 and 3 are very similar to God's judgment of the earth
(ץרא, BDB 75) in Noah's day (cf. Genesis 6-9;
also note the attempts to avoid God's judgment in Isa. 2:10,19,21). Worldwide emptying is
exactly the opposite of creation's purpose!

SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH

▣ "distorts its surface" This could either be imagery of God's judgment on the earth in
physical terms (lit. "twist," BDB 730, KB 796, Piel PERFECT with waw) or it may
be imagery of God emptying earth's inhabitants as someone would clean dirty kitchen pans.

▣ "and scatters its inhabitants" This is very similar to the terminology used in Genesis 10 for
the tower of Babel. Here it denotes exile.

24:2 This shows that all social distinctions are removed. Everyone is judged (cf. Isa. 24:4).

24:3 "for the Lord has spoken this word" This shows the certainty of
this event because God has said it (BDB 180, KB 210, Piel PERFECT, cf. Isa. 24:3; 25:8;
40:8; 55:10-11). Also note the intended contrast; the spoken word of creation is now the spoken word of judgment.

24:4 Note the description of the earth (both erets [BDB 75] and tebel [BDB 385]) .

- mourns

- BDB 5 I, KB 6, Qal PERFECT, cf. Jer. 23:10; for the
personification of the earth, also note Isa. 24:7

- BDB 5 II means "dry up," which fits the parallelism of Isa. 24:4 and 7 better (cf. NRSV, REB)

- withers ‒ BDB 615, KB 663, Qal PERFECT (twice)

- fades ‒ BDB 51, KB 63, Pulal PERFECT, cf. Isa. 16:8; 33:9

- polluted, Isa. 24:5 ‒ BDB 337, KB 335, Qal PERFECT

Notice the number of PERFECT VERBS in Isa. 24:4 and 5 that denote
a settled action, a complete action! All of these VERBS have a sound similarity.

The God of creation is acting as sovereign in His creation. It was made to be a stage for Him
and mankind to interact, but His creatures have polluted and defiled it by their choices and actions. The planet was
created for abundance (i.e. Gen. 1), but now lies judged and unproductive.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣ "the world" This Hebrew term (BDB 385) is often used in conjunction with "earth" (BDB 75,
cf. Job 37:12; Ps. 96:13; 98:9; Jer. 10:12; Lam. 4:12, see
SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH). Isaiah
uses this word more than any other prophet (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 273, cf. Isa. 13:11; 24:4; 34:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORLD (several terms)

▣ "the exalted of the people of the earth fade away" The RSV translation (with a change of vowels
only) implies that this phrase relates to the judgment of heaven and earth (i.e. all creation, cf. v., 21 and footnote in JPSOA),
not to the elite (i.e. "height") people of the earth only. The UBS Text Project, p. 56, thinks the MT is not the original
text and agrees witht the RSV version.

24:5 "The earth is also polluted by its inhabitants" Nature suffers because of mankind's sin (cf. Isa. 24:20;
Gen. 3:17-19; Num. 35:33; Jer. 3:1-2,9; Rom. 8:18-25).

- they transgressed laws, BDB 716, KB 778, Qal PERFECT

- they violated statutes, BDB 322, KB 321, Qal PERFECT

- they broke the everlasting covenant, BDB 830, KB 974, Hiphil PERFECT

This does not refer to the Mosaic Law, but either

- to the natural revelation found in Ps. 19:1-6 and Rom. 1:19, 20; 2:14-15

- to Noah's day (cf. Gen. 6:5-7,11-12, possibly specifically to 9:4-6, which is supported by JPSOA footnote)

The same phrase "everlasting covenant" appears in Gen. 9:16. This everlasting covenant would
relate to the taking of human life (cf. Isa. 26:21). Murder has consequences! Life belongs to God. He
wants mankind to be fruitful and fill the earth, not kill each other!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam and aiōnios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

24:6 "a curse devours the earth" This sounds very similar to the curse of Gen. 3:17-19. Theologically
this functions like Rom. 1:18-3:20; all have sinned (i.e. broken a covenant, cf. Isa. 24:5) and need God's
salvation!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HITTITE (Suzerain) TREATIES

NASB, NKJV, JB
"are burned"

NKJV
"dwindled"

REB
"dwindle"

Peshitta
"shall be destroyed"

LXX
"shall be poor"

DSS
"grow pale" (from BDB 301 I, cf. Isa. 29:22)

JPSOA
"consumes"

The MT has "burned" (BDB 359 I, KB 357 or 351 I, Qal PERFECT).
Scholars have suggested another possible Arab root, "to reduce" (KB 351 II), which matches the next phrase.

This is a good example of the difficulty in ambiguous Hebrew poetry. Context often is an
interpreter's only safe guide and even then, other roots and cognates are possible. The MT is not the
earliest Hebrew text.

▣ "and few men are left" This is basically the OT idea of a faithful remnant that God will spare
a few of the people of the earth. This sounds very similar to Jesus' words in Matt. 7:14.

24:7-14 This is a series images about the normal social activities of an agricultural community
which is brought to an end because of the judgment of God.

24:9 "wine. . .strong drink" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: WINE AND STRONG DRINK.

24:10 "The city of chaos is broken down" There is a play throughout this literary unit on "a city." It is
not specifically identified and, therefore, seems to be a symbol of all human society functioning apart
from God (similar to the city of Genesis 11).

This city can be seen in Isa. 25:2,3,12. An allusion to God's city is found in Isa. 26:1-6
(cf. Heb. 11:10,16).

Literally, the term "chaos" (BDB 1062) means "emptiness," "vanity," "formlessness," "confusion,"
or "unreality" used to describe the earth in Genesis 1:2 ("formless"). It is used often in Isaiah
(cf. Isa. 24:10; 29:21; 34:11; 40:17,23; 41:29; 44:9; 45:18,19; 49:4; 59:4), but only one other time in
all the Prophets (i.e. Jer. 4:23). God started over with His creation with Noah (Genesis 6-9), now He
will do it again!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TWO CITIES IN ISAIAH

24:12 "the gate is battered to ruins" The VERB (BDB 510,
KB 507, Hophal IMPERFECT) denotes that "the unidentified city"
is defenseless, her gates are in ruins! Who can stand before YHWH?

24:13 "For thus it will be in the midst of the earth among the peoples" This could be interpreted in
two ways:

- it could refer to all of the people of the earth (cf. Isa. 24:1 and Isa. 11:10 )

- it could refer to the scattered Jews of the Exile (cf. Isa. 11:11)

It is difficult to make a decision on this point, but it seems to me that because of Isa. 24:14,16
and 25:6,7, we are talking about the universal worldview/message (i.e. option #1) so characteristic of Isaiah
(cf. Isa. 2:2-4; 12:4-5; 25:6-9; 42:6-12; 45:22-23; 49:5-6; 51:4-5; 60:1-3; 66:23)! This universal redemption purpose
is very specific in its invitation to both Egypt and Assyria to be a part of God's Kingdom in Isa. 19:18-25.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "As the shaking of an olive tree,

As the gleanings when the grape harvest is over"

This was agricultural imagery for harvesting. It denotes the fact that there will be very
few people left (cf. Isa. 24:6; Mic. 7:1). Verses 14-16 are a praise unit referring to those who trust YHWH. It
is characteristic of this literary unit and this particular kind of genre in Isaiah to promise blessings
right in the midst of judgment.

24:14-15 "west. . .east" The term "west" (BDB 410) is literally "sea" and refers to the Mediterranean
Ocean.

The term "east" (BDB 22) is literally "light" which refers to the rising of the sun. Again, these
two terms may be imagery for Egypt to the west and Assyria to the east (cf. Isa. 19:23-25).

24:15 The Jewish Study Bible, p. 830, asserts that some group (Judeans or Gentiles who have trusted
YHWH, Isa. 24:15,16a; 25:3) begins to thank God in praise (Isa. 24:14) that the judgment is over, but they
suddenly realize it is not (cf. Isa. 24:16b-23).

Recognizing the majesty and glory of YHWH is obviously the first sign of a new relationship
with Him (cf. Isa. 12:5; 26:10). A few humans (Jew and Gentile), the faithful remnant (cf. Isa. 24:6; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT [three senses]) will be found
faithful even amidst judgment (cf. Hab. 2:4).

▣ "in the coastlands of the sea" In the LXX this is "the islands," which is usually a reference
within Isaiah to Gentiles (cf. Isa. 41:5; 42:4,10).

24:16a This is another reference to the universal aspect of the inclusion of Gentile believers
(cf. Isa. 2:2-4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

"the righteous"

"the Upright One"

The NASB, NRSV, NJB, and NET translations take this phrase to denote Israel's God. The Peshitta,
KJV, and ASV have "the righteous," which is another reference to the believing remnant which will be saved out of
Israel and the peoples of the earth. The TEV and REB has "the righteous nation," apparently the ideal Israel.

24:16b There is an obvious break here which is not clearly marked by the traditional verse divisions.
From the obvious praise section of Isa. 24:14-16a, Isa. 24:16b begins a funeral dirge relating to the
coming judgment of God (note "woe" [twice, lit. "I pine or waste away"] and "woe,"
the INTERJECTION, BDB 17). Its exact relation to the context is somewhat
uncertain. It may be a personal comment of Isaiah himself that his own day did not fit, Isa. 24:14-16a.
There have been many different English translations of this phrase.

The AB Commentary (p. 353) notes that this phrase is omitted by the Septuagint and the author
(Blenkinsop) assumes the Aramaic root for "secret," which follows rabbinical tradition (see footnote in JPSOA) and
the Peshitta and Vulgate versions.

24:16c,d "Treacherous. . .traeacherously" (twice) This is a very powerful word play. There are several
uses of one word (BDB 93, KB 108), which has a powerful, repetitious emphasis on the faithless, deceitful
people. Note

- the treacherous, BDB 93, KB 108, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE

- deal treacherously, BDB 93, KB 108, Qal PERFECT

- NOUN, BDB 93 I (cf. Jer. 12:1)

- repeat of #1

- repeat of #2

24:17 "Terror and pit and snare" This is a sound play on similar words. All of these words (BDB 808,
809, 809) are used of trapping animals (cf. Jer. 48:43,44).

▣ "will fall into the pit. . .will be caught in the snare" These are allusions to humans being
trapped like animals (cf. Isa. 8:15; 28:13). Humans will try to flee God's judgment only to find
disaster (cf. Isa. 2:10,19-22).

24:18c "the windows above are opened" This is another allusion to the flood account of Genesis 6-9
(cf. Isa. 7:11; 8:2). The opening of the windows of heaven can be for

- blessing (i.e. water for agriculture and flocks, cf. 2 Kgs. 7:2,19; Mal. 3:10)

- judgment (i.e. sending of too much water, cf. Gen. 7:11; 8:2; Isa. 24:18, or no water)

The earth was created by God for a place to meet and fellowship with mankind (i.e. Gen. 3:8).
It was created for abundance and life; it has become ruin and will be destroyed

- by water, Genesis 6-9

- by the spoken word, Isa. 24:3

- by apocalyptic imagery, Jer. 4:23-28

- by fire, 2 Pet. 3:10-11

24:20 Drunkenness (i.e. staggering, BDB 631, KB 681, INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root) is often used as a symbol for judgment
in the OT (cf. Isa. 19:14; 28:7,8; 29:9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WINE AND STRONG DRINK

▣ "And it totters like a shack" This is another cultural allusion to a small booth (BDB 434)
which was built in the field during harvest time for someone to live so he could protect the harvest (cf. Isa. 1:8).

Isaiah 24:19-20 describes the sin-laden physical creation (cf. Rom. 3:9-18,23; 8:18-22).

▣ "never to rise again" This is a hyperbolic statement to show the intensity of God's judgment
on a morally polluted earth. But from other texts, we know He will have mercy on it and restore it! For
the use of hyperbolic language in both prophecy and apocalyptic literature see D. Brent Sandy,
Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic.

24:21 "in that day" See note at Isa. 2:11. This eschatological theme marker is repeated in Isa. 25:9;
26:1,2,12.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE LAST DAYS

▣ "the host of heaven" Many times in the OT this refers to the Babylonian astral deities
(cf. Isa. 40:26; 45:12). However, in this context it refers to the OT concept of the angels of the nations
(cf. Deut. 32:8 in the LXX and Daniel 10). God will judge both the human beings (i.e. "on earth") who rebel
against Him and also the angels (i.e. "on high") who have aided in either the human rebellion or satanic temptation
(see G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, p. 179).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

24:22 Both the prideful and arrogant kings of the earth (cf. Isa. 10:12; 13:11) and the national
rebellious angels (cf. LXX of Deut. 32:8 and Dan. 10:10-13) will be judged and imprisoned. This is very
similar to 2 Pet. 2:4; Jude; and Rev. 20:1-3. This seems to be an allusion to Sheol (OT)
or Tartarus (NT).

Some scholars have asserted that "after many days" refers to the millennium of Rev. 20:1-6.
This is typical of millennial scholars who desperately seek some biblical evidence for the time frame mentioned
only in Revelation 20. See my new written Commentary on Revelation 20 (Partial Preterist) at
www.freebiblecommentary.org.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?

▣ "prisoners" This form (BDB 64) is found only here and it is missing in the DSS, the LXX,
and the Aramaic Targums.

24:23 "the moon will be abashed and the sun ashamed" This is apocalyptic language speaking of the
cataclysmic events within nature as the Creator approaches. The presence of the Lord
Himself will become the light for mankind (cf. Isa. 30:26; 60:19, 20; Rev. 21:23; 22:5). See my new exegetical
Commentary on Revelation (2024).

▣ "the Lord of hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem" Here
again is the universal aspect of all the world flowing unto Jerusalem to know the one true God
(cf. Isa. 2:2-4; 24:23; 25:6-7; 27:6, 13). This imagery is focused on YHWH's reign over all the
earth in Dan. 2:35,44-45!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "His glory will be before His elders" The elders (BDB 278) were leaders in Moses' day
(i.e. Exod. 3:16,18; 4:29; 12:21, etc.). The term denoted older men of the different tribes. It came
to stand for all civil leadership. In Isaiah the elders are irresponsible (cf. Isa. 3:2-3; 9:14-16), but
here in the eschaton they will behold YHWH's glory (presumably in worship and adoration, i.e. redeemed
elders).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible
for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy
Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Why is Isa. 24-27 called apocalyptic?

- From what OT passage does Isaiah draw his imagery?

- How is the faithful city of Isa. 1:26 related to the city of chaos in Isa. 24:10?

- Who speaks in Isa. 24:14-16a and who in Isa. 24:16b?

- Who are the "hosts of heaven" (lit. "the host of the height in the height")?
